content.title: About
content.content: Dal refers to dried legumes such as lentils, split peas, mung beans, and various types of beans that are staples in South Asian, Middle Eastern and African cuisines. They are rich in protein, fiber and complex carbohydrates, have a mild nutty flavor and are usually cooked by boiling or simmering.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “dal” comes from the Sanskrit “dāl”, meaning “legume”.
India alone cultivates more than 50 varieties of dal, differing in color, shape and taste.
Dal is a primary source of plant‑based protein in many vegetarian diets.
When cooked, dal expands 2–3 times its dry volume, making storage easy.
Traditionally dal is served with rice or flatbreads such as chapati or naan.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Dal provides 20–25 % protein, making it an important amino‑acid source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from dal is better absorbed when paired with vitamin C (e.g., tomatoes).

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Dal raises blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B6 and folate support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Raw legumes contain phytic acid and lectins that can hinder mineral absorption; soaking and cooking reduce them.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause flatulence; proper soaking and cooking minimize this effect.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit legume intake due to higher purine levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse dal, soak it (typically 4–8 hours), then boil until tender. Use it in soups, curries, purees, salads or as a side dish. It can be made into dal‑puri, dal‑tadka or added to vegetable stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry dal in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, it remains good for up to 1 year. Cooked dal should be refrigerated and consumed within 3–4 days.
